chapter: Armstrong, Parker and life inside the Basie band
title: Billie Love at Armstrong's dance and her death
summary: A young woman throws her undergarment onto Armstrong's horn during Body and Soul and dies hours later; Armstrong remembers it later.

story.theme_name: Working with and around Louis Armstrong
story.community_name: Playing with and around Louis Armstrong

blocks.x: So he let us all off and the T. found a band and we all went to hear Louie and that was really the first time I really heard him in person. He had a big band, about -- I think he had about 12, 13 piece band then. But he was really sharp that night and there used to be a little girl that lived just across the room from me in the hotel. She came down there to study. She was having a problem at home, very nice girl, very beautiful girl. Everybody had eyes, but nobody could really make her, you know, they never really made her. Her name was Billie Love I'll never forget.

I used to go sit and talk with her at night. She says, 'Buddy,' she says, 'you know, the reason I'm away from home, I can't study at home. My mother and dad --' they were having some kind of little problems and it was interfering with her thinking, you know. And she says, 'But if I would go with anybody, it would maybe be you, but I'm not going to do it.'

So that night, the first time I ever seen it, she got drunk. And she made Louie's dance and Louie played 'Body and Soul' and sang 'Body and Soul.' She was standing in front of the bandstand and she just pulled her pants off and threw them up and luckily, they landed right on the bell of his horn. Pop said, 'I can't do nothing with these, baby,' you know how he'd go into his little thing, because he had one of his wives sitting --

I think it was Alma or Velma, one of those wives. And this is the truth. She was stoned. I think it was the first time she ever had a drink in her life. And two hours later -- she went on home, you know, like after the dance, and two hours after that, she died, went home and died that night. And she wasn't -- I guess she was about 17, 18 years old. And it was really a big shock. And in later years -- well, they called it acute indigestion, but it must have been a heart attack or something, you know. But it really,

you know, it was upsetting, it upset everybody. In later years, after I came to New York with Basie, I asked -- I reminded Louie of it. I says, "Pops, you remember that night, the first time I met you in Tulsa? We sat out and talked about four or five --" I talked to him about four or five hours, Gary, just talking. And I says, "You remember that time?" He says, "Yeah, I told you you'd make it to New York." I says, "You remember when you played 'Body and Soul' and that little beautiful girl down there pulled her panties off and threw them up on the bell?" He said, "Man, wasn't that a fine chick? Yeah, I remember that." So I said, "Wasn't she beautiful?" He says, "She sure was, man." But he says, "There wasn't nothing I could do. I had my wife sitting on the bandstand." I said -- well, he didn't know this. I says, "Well, two hours later, she died." And that really upset him, you know? He didn't know that, you know, like they left that night. But that was the truth.
